summary: LunaWindow is a free, open-source web app that answers the key question of this challenge: where and when can a lander survive at the Moon's south pole? For any point on the Moon and any date from 1960 to 2099, it computes three needs over the mission period: sunlight for power, a direct radio link with Earth, and the longest night the batteries must survive. Sun and Earth positions come from NAIF SPICE (JPL DE440) and terrain horizons from LRO LOLA elevation models, validated against JPL Horizons and NASA PGDA illumination maps. Instead of a complex interface, users explore a 3D Moon, see a clear verdict with the reason behind each need, slip the launch date, compare two dates side by side and stand on the surface in a 3D view with the real terrain, Sun and Earth. A Challenge mode with six missions turns it into a learning tool for students, teachers and the public. It runs in any browser, including phones, with no installation or account: https://lunawindow.vercel.app (mirror: https://komasan19283645.github.io/LunaWindow/)
details:
What it does

LunaWindow is an interactive 3D Moon in the browser that helps users decide where and when to land at the lunar south pole. For any point on the Moon and any UTC date from 1960 to 2099, it computes the three needs that decide whether a lander survives over a 7, 14 or 28-day mission:

  • Power: the share of the period with any part of the Sun's disc above the local terrain horizon.
  • Earth link: the share of the period with the Earth above the same horizon, for direct-to-Earth communication.
  • Night: the longest unbroken stretch without sunlight, which sets the battery requirement.

The app turns these numbers into a clear verdict (Mission ready, Almost there, Not yet), explains why each need fails (which ridge hides the Sun or the Earth, in which direction and how high, and when the longest gap starts) and suggests what to try next. It has two modes over the same engine:

  • Explore: live dials, a timeline with sunlight and Earth bands, launch-slip buttons, a comparison tray, a split screen to compare two dates, and a 3D view from the landing site with the real terrain, the Sun and the Earth at their true angular size and the lander in place.
  • Challenge: six missions with the aids hidden. Users pick a site and a launch day, watch the landing and earn up to three stars and a mission patch.

How it works

  • Sun and Earth positions: NAIF SPICE kernels (JPL DE440 and the lunar orientation frame) give the sub-solar and sub-Earth points every 12 hours from 1960 to 2099; the browser interpolates this table and computes azimuth and elevation at the site.
  • Terrain horizon: rays traced over NASA LRO LOLA elevation models (5 m/px near polar sites, then 20 m and 240 m) from an antenna 2 m above the ground give the horizon in 720 directions. Any point the user clicks gets its own horizon computed in the browser.
  • Visibility: each hour of the period is compared with the horizon; rise and set times are refined to the minute.
  • Catalogue: 12 real sites, including the Artemis III candidate regions, the IM-1 and IM-2 landing points, Blue Ghost M1, Apollo 11 and Apollo 17.

Benefits and validation

The challenge notes that existing tools are powerful but hard for non-specialists. LunaWindow keeps the real numbers and explains them in plain language. Its accuracy is measured, not assumed: Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons within 0.0002° over 2,736 test instants; LOLA heights match NAIF landing-site altitudes within 0.5 to 10.5 m; and mean Earth and Sun visibility over an 18.6-year cycle match NASA PGDA illumination maps within 2.3 and 4.2 percentage points on average.

Education: inspiring the Artemis generation

Education is at the heart of LunaWindow. With Artemis, NASA is preparing a sustained human presence on and around the Moon, and today's students are the engineers, scientists and astronauts who will carry it forward. LunaWindow is designed to spark that vocation:

  • Active learning: students do not memorise facts; they make decisions (a site, a launch date), test them and see the consequences.
  • Learning through play: the Challenge mode turns real mission planning into six missions with stars and mission patches, so the app feels like a game while every number is real NASA data.
  • Immediate, explained feedback: every result says what went wrong, why and what to try next, so mistakes become lessons.
  • Cross-curricular: it connects physics, mathematics, geography, astronomy and technology (Sun angles, latitude, day and night cycles, communication geometry) through one motivating question.
  • Ready for the classroom: free, open source and browser-based, on phones too, with no account; teachers can share a link to an exact scenario.
  • Real data, real missions: students work with the same sites NASA is studying for Artemis III and the same data sources mission planners use.

Intended impact

Students, teachers and the public learn, by doing, why the lunar south pole is both attractive and difficult: long days and nights, a Sun that skims the horizon and ridges that block the Earth. Teachers can share a link to a ready scenario or use the six missions in class. Mission planners get a fast way to compare sites and dates before using specialist tools.

Institutional support

LunaWindow is backed by the university and by secondary education:

  • César Sánchez Meléndez, Vice-Rector for Culture, Sport and Social Commitment, University of Castilla-La Mancha (UCLM): institutional support and a commitment to help disseminate the project.
  • Miguel Ángel López Guerrero, Full Professor of Applied Mathematics, UCLM: describes it as serious work, with a well-posed problem and a solid base in real NASA data and the validation against JPL Horizons, and supports its dissemination.
  • Marina Lloret Galerón, technology teacher at IES Marcos Zaragoza (Villajoyosa, Alicante): finds the idea interesting and useful thanks to its game-like interface, plans to use it with her students, and suggested exporting data to a spreadsheet for classroom problems, which is on our roadmap.

The original messages are shown below and in the project repository: https://github.com/Komasan19283645/LunaWindow#institutional-support

Tools and technologies

  • Web app: JavaScript and TypeScript, three.js, Vite.
  • Science engine: TypeScript with 113 automated tests.
  • Data processing and validation: Python, SpiceyPy (NAIF SPICE), NumPy, rasterio, FastAPI.
  • Deployment: Vercel (static site), Docker and Render (optional API), GitHub Actions for continuous integration.
  • Hardware: none required; it runs in any desktop or mobile browser with WebGL.

Creativity

  • It does not just score a site: it explains what went wrong and why, so users learn instead of guessing.
  • Time is a first-class choice: the same site can succeed or fail depending on the launch date, and the split screen shows both in 3D.
  • Users can stand at the landing site and see the real horizon, Sun and Earth as the lander would.
  • Any point on the Moon can be analysed, not only a fixed list of sites.

Factors we considered

  • Audience: accessible to students and the public without hiding the real data.
  • Scientific honesty: NASA publishes Artemis III regions as areas of about 15 × 15 km, so LunaWindow analyses the highest landable point of each (slope ≤ 8° over 50 m), the best case for illumination, and states it clearly. Boulders below the elevation model resolution, the lander's own shadow, solar-panel performance and refraction are not modelled.
  • Performance and access: all data fits in 18 MB and every calculation runs in the browser, with no server, installation or account.
  • Accessibility: plain English with a glossary, large text and strong contrast.
